utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I would like to put on the record that the videolink which was granted for witnesses IC-01 and IC-02 has become moot because both witnesses have been withdrawn from the witness list by the Cermak Defence. Then I -- there was a matter where the Prosecution was due to inform the Chamber today, Mr. Waespi, not to be done in open court, but do you have any idea on when you would want to inform the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a written affidavit or declaration by the investigator which I could file or deal with any way you deem appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that during the first break. Thank you. Then is the Cermak Defence ready to call its next witness, which I understand would be -- and apparently without protective measures, would be Emin Teskeredzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam -- Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Teskeredzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Teskeredzic. Please be seated. Mr. Teskeredzic, you will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Teskeredzic.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Teskeredzic, I'd like you to look at the screen to your right, and I'm going to ask to you look at a document that will come onto the screen, which is 2D00724. This is a statement that you signed for the Defence, and I want you to identify it. Can you see there on the right-hand side of the screen a statement -- [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, can I. I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... down at the bottom so that we can see your signature on it. Do you identify your signature?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps now if we could look at the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And can you see there your signature at the end of the document, next to the date of the 26th of May, 2009?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in between each page is signed by Mr. Teskeredzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Teskeredzic, when you gave that statement to the Defence and signed that statement, did you have an opportunity to read through it and confirm the contents?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I confirmed the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is everything that you have said in that statement, to the best of your knowledge and belief, true and correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I was to ask you in court today the same questions in respect of which you gave answers that gave the information in this statement, would those answers be the same today?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In those circumstances, Your Honour, I ask that this statement be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1732. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1732 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will give a brief summary of the statement before I go on to ask Mr. Teskeredzic some further questions. Mr. Teskeredzic is, by occupation, someone involved in research, in relation to maritime science. During the conflict in the former Yugoslavia he worked with a team in work of de-mining explosives. He worked for a waterborne operations unit, and his experience in working in the decommissioning of mines and explosions caused him to work in various areas of the conflict between 1992 and 1995. At the time of Operation Oluja, he was not mobilized and was on holiday; but after hearing of the liberation of the occupied territories and hearing of the appointment of Mr. Cermak as the commander of the garrison in the town of Knin, he contacted Mr. Cermak an offered his services to help him in normalising life in Knin by decommissioning any booby-traps, mines, or explosives that may have been left behind by the RSK forces who had occupied the area previously. He contacted former members of his unit. He went to Knin and set about that kind of work on behalf of the community working for Mr. Cermak as required as well as Mr. Pasic. Because of his experience in fish and maritime matters, he also, with the help of others, restored the fish farm in Knin to enable it to operate for the benefit of the town. And during his work for Mr. Cermak and Knin, he undertook various operations whereby he was de-mining areas outside the town to make various public installations safe. Your Honour, that's the summary of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Teskeredzic, I'm now going ask you some specific questions in relation to your evidence. And is it correct that at the time of Operation Oluja, you were not in fact mobilized?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you voluntarily contact Mr. Cermak to see if you could give him any help in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did Mr. Cermak accept your offer of assistance?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you contact members of your former unit to establish whether they would be able to come and help you in your work in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I contacted them and made arrangements with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did they come and join you over the next few days and operate with you in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and they operated with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to your work in munitions de-mining, what were the particular matters that you were concerned with in Knin at this time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Specifically, we checked the railway lines, specific facilities. We found a storage place close to the railway line; we emptied it. We transferred the contents to the military depot. We followed the railway line toward Zadar and toward Gracac. Individuals would approach us who had returned -- who wanted to return to their homes and wanted to us check if the area was safe. We also had to check the electricity grid facilities, including electricity posts, which we had to check the safety of before electricity workers could commence their work, so that the electricity supply would be restored to Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After a period of time, were steps taken by you and Mr. Cermak to have you officially mobilized, in relation to your work in the area?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He sent a request to my institute, asking that I be relieved of my duties for a certain period of time, and he did the same for my associates, who were there working with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit D1027, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A document is going to come up on the right-hand screen again. Mr. Teskeredzic, I'd like you to look at that document in your own language. It's dated the 19th of August, 1995. It's signed by Mr. Cermak. And it's addressed to the Rudjer Boskovic Institute in Zagreb. First of all, can you confirm that the Rudjer Boskovic institute in Zagreb was the place where you were working at that time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I worked for the Institute at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And are you currently working there now, in fact?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see here that its subject is request for relief from employment, and it reads about the exceptional need to organise pyrotechnical clearance of the terrain and facilities and removal of mine and explosive devices and ammunition. And we can see that it states that had you been carrying out the activities since the 6th of August, and a request is made to relieve you from your employment until further notice. Did you see this letter at the time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was it your idea or Mr. Cermak's idea that it should be written to the Institute?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: The idea was mine. I was on annual leave for a while, and I was supposed to report back to work. So my status had to be settled, in a way, and it was done through the request addressed to the Institute to relieve me of my permanent duties so that I may attend to the duties I had in Knin at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could now turn to Exhibit D1026.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is another letter dated the 19th of August, 1995, sent by Mr. Cermak to the Ministry of Defence in Zagreb, mobilisation administration, and is a request for mobilisation in relation to the work we described of you, a Colonel Domancic, and Lieutenant Tomsic. And were you aware of that letter being written at that time by Mr. Cermak, requesting your mobilisation by the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Colonel Domancic, Lieutenant Tomsic; what was your connection with them?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: They were members of the same unit that I was previously. And Domancic was my deputy, and he was a top-notch explosives expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next document, D1028.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could just look at this document. It's from the Split Military District Command, Knin forward command post, dated the 6th of September. Subject: Mobilisation of servicemen. Our response to the Knin garrison, signed by General Gotovina. And we can see the information in the letter, but it's the last sentence, the Defence minister did not agree to the mobilisation of the requested individuals. Were you aware that the minister of defence had refused the initial request to mobilise you and your colleagues made by Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could now look to the next document, 2D00254. It's a letter dated the 11th of September, 1995. It's from the Knin garrison by Mr. Cermak and addressed to the minister of defence in Zagreb, Mr. Susak. And its subject is a request. And were -- we can see from the letter written there that, because of the need for de-mining terrain structures, we were forced during Operation Storm to take de-miners without a mobilisation call-up, for whom we later issued mobilisation call-ups, dated the 4th of September ... It's stated that the letter we've just looked at on the 6th of September denied the request and that the minister of defence had not given his approval. And then the last paragraph: Since the - it's got military conscripts here - are still in the field and are necessary, due to the extent of the work and their expertise, they cannot be paid a salary until they receive your approval. And the request is made for the mobilisation. Were you aware that General Cermak had written to Minister Susak to try and obtain the mobilisation of you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I know that he took steps to have us mobilised. Now, who he wrote to in the process, I don't know. We had a great deal of work to do, and I simply did not give it any thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at page 2 of the letter, we will see a list of de-miners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you recognise the names there? Of course, not only your own, but of the others? Were they part of your team?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can now go to -- oh, Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become Exhibit D1733. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1733 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document I'd like us to look at is 65 ter 4635.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a letter dated the 18th of September, 1995, from the Administration for Compulsory Military Service and Mobilisation sent to the Knin garrison. And we can see that on that date the letter says, based on the Article 55 that the Ministry of Defence approved the request of garrison an ordered the mobilisation of four of the listed people, including yourself. The name Drago Margus is missing from the previous list. Are you able to help why his name was missing from this list?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Probably because he worked in -- at the fish breeding farm most of the time and did not engage in mine clearance on -- to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can see what the letter says, about the report that is required to be submitted after completion of mobilisation. And that they were to be received by General Cermak and the various addressees, including Split Military District Command that this was addressed to. Thank you. If we could now turn to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections if it's to be tendered, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah, I was calling up the next one while I was going to then tender it. Can that document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit D1734. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have -- sorry, Your Honour. Can we have Exhibit D767, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document is dated the 20th of September, 1995, from the Split Military District Command, Knin forward command post, to the Knin garrison. And, again, pursuant to Article 55 of the Law on Defence, the order is made. The following may be mobilized for Military Post 3231, Knin. And we see the list of names there, this time including Drago Margus, to be mobilized, to report to the Knin garrison, to be received by Colonel -- General Cermak. And when mobilisation has been implemented, a report was to be sent to the Split Military District Command, section for mobilisation, Knin forward command post. And the end of the letter -- order says: Following the execution of the tasks planned - this is on page 3 - demobilize conscript, issue them with certificates, and inform the responsible defence offices where the conscripts' records are kept of this, signed by General Gotovina. Were you aware at that time that the mobilisation was eventually granted by the Minister of Defence, Mr. Susak, as well as by General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Was a report on the work of the explosive ordnance disposal team for the period from August to September 1995 filed by you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: There was a report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can look at Exhibit D1030.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Mr. Kay, I didn't find the 18th of September approval, which is now D1734 on your exhibit list to be used. Was it on your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's on the Prosecution 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the Prosecution 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But not for this witness. It's on the general 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I take it, then, Mr. Waespi, that no objections would include the introduction of the document as a potential exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- in view of my question, I would have expected a yes. But I took it that there would be no objection and no means here no objection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have, on our screen in front of us, a report dated the 22nd of September, 1995, and we see the list of names there. Were those the individuals who made up your team, in relation to the ordnance disposal work?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we look at the work that's itemised there, we see the railway, hydroelectric power, diary, trout farm in Srb. Trout farm, Krcic; Knin; Gips; Tvik; and various other places, institutions. Was that work the work that you and your team had undertaken?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the sort of work we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Civilian facilities identified. Military facilities. Kosovo warehouses in Kosovo. What were those warehouses? Can you remember what those facilities were?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: These were military facilities along the Krka river. One of the military facilities was Vitorog relay centre. There was a large amount of explosive there. There were 15 trenches with the 400 kilos of explosive -- explosives. There was a train we found in a tunnel that was loaded with explosives. There was another warehouse at Bender, up at the railway station above Knin close to a private home, where we found a great amount of explosives that were transported to Knin, and from there on to Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned Bender. Can you describe what you did in relation to Bender, how those munitions were discovered, and how you went there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: When we were checking the railway line, we came across the storage facility. We had to walk along the railway line, and as we found the storage place or the warehouse we went back to Knin to seek assistance from Mr. Cermak, in terms of organising means of transport. There were 70 to 80 tons of ammunitions that we found up there. We had maps, since we weren't that sure of the route we were supposed to take. Mr. Cermak organised for Mr. Pero Pasic to accompany us. He hailed from that particular place, and he knew his way there. So it took us two or three trips to load all of the ammunitions, and I believe that we have a record stating exactly the amount of explosives found there and what sort of ammunition it involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'd like to look at Exhibit D763, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document headed order from the Knin garrison, signed by General Cermak. And it refers to the urgent clearing of the military depot in Plavno, and with the aim of making the return of the population to this settlement as flexible and fast as possible. "And I hereby issue the following order. Clear the facility and the terrain in the village of Plavno as urgently as possible. Person responsible, Lieutenant Vuk. "Make the mines and explosives," et cetera, "in the warehouse the priority. Person responsible: Lieutenant Vuk." And a commission was appointed, including you and a report to be filed after the task, and the resources should be transferred to the section of the logistics base in Sibenik. Does this order from General Cermak relate to that munitions that you were describing as being found near Knin?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to Exhibit D1020.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see the report from Colonel Frkic on the confiscation of the materiel and equipment from the railway station depot, Plavno-Benderi hamlet to General Cermak. And describes going to Bender and finding weapons and munition and that it was taken away to the 306th Logistics Base in Sibenik. Is that correct, as a description in this report, as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said there was munitions and explosives found here. What -- what would be -- what was the quantity, what was the scale of the discovery of munitions found in this place?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a military depot but, rather, a building belonging to a cooperative or something like. There were Zoljas, there were machine-guns, ammunitions, and hand-grenades. We made the exact list. I can't remember anymore how much we found of each type of explosive, but there were about 80 tons altogether. We had to take two truck-loads. We couldn't transport it all at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we look at the next page, we see a list. Just cast your eye down that to look at the type of munitions that were found. We can see a hand-held rocket-launcher, rocket, grenades, shells. If we turn to page 2 now, we see further munitions. Where -- was this materiel held in a secure way? How was it held in this building?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: It was kept -- the cellar of that building. I can't say that the place was too secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did this kind of materiel being in the area at the time, was that a danger?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a great danger. Even we felt insecure, because there could have been a booby-trap in any of those cases, and we could have all been blown up. So it was a very dangerous job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could now look at Exhibit D765.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, could I just seek one piece of clarification on this list. Under number 2 it reads 64 millimetre M-80 Zolja RBR. Was that ammunition, or were these rocket-launchers; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were rocket-launchers, hand-held rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is the quantity there 158? I would move from the page, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we just go back to the second page. Oh, if it's ... I'm sorry, I didn't realize we'd moved on. Your Honour, we -- took us back and the other document was already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, the Croatian has 158 ... Thank you. Yeah, well, we can see that, no question arises. Can we go back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, however the -- the list says that there were 158 boxes. The unit being a box, the quantity being 158. Does that mean that there were 158 boxes containing Zolja hand-held rocket-launchers, Mr. Teskeredzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believe that there were 158 pieces of these rocket-launchers, but I can't really remember exactly. There was a huge amount of everything there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said there was a huge amount of everything. But this out as the second -- no, third highest number of equipment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were that many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And just looking at number 3, 82-millimetre M-60 BST recoilless gun rocket, 22. Is that 22 recoilless gun rockets or shells or bullets, whatever they are?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not an answer to the question, I'm afraid. Is this -- let me just check first. Yes, so that is -- perhaps it is an answer, but perhaps I'm not sufficiently familiar. That means that it is 22 rockets to be fired by a recoilless gun. Is that how I have to understand item number 3 on this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the rest is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we go to Exhibit D765.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We can see here a request for temporary transfer written on the 22nd of August by General Cermak to Colonel General Cuk of the 1st Croatian Guards Corps. And referring to the exceptional need to carry out explosive ordnance clearing of terrain and facilities. And then requesting Major Vuk, Lieutenant Plemencic, Junior Lieutenant Perkovic to be transferred to the garrison as the individuals, as per a request dated the 8th of August, 1995, were engaged in the work. And Colonel Gregorovic was informed of this request on 15th of August and the matter needed to be resolved promptly and requesting the temporary transfer of two More, Lieutenant Teskeredzic, Staff-sergeant Halas. Were you aware at the time of Mr. Cermak also seeking other members to be involved with the ordnance clearing, including a Lieutenant Teskeredzic?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is Lieutenant Teskeredzic related to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And was he involved in ordnance clearance as well?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also file further reports on the clearing of the Vitorog railway relay junction?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can see Exhibit D1031.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was this a report filed by you concerning the Vitorog relay junction?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No further questions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving now to other work, did you become involved in the repair of the fish farm in Knin?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my area of expertise, and this is where I could help most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What did you discover in relation to the fish farm? What was its condition and state?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: The fish farm needs to be cleaned. The screens need to be cleaned every day. When you breed trouts, the water needs to circulate up to 120 times a day, so you need a large quantity of water. Once you stop this circulation of water, once the screens are filled with leaves or any other material, the fish start to die. So we needed to establish the normal conditions as soon as possible, to prevent fish from dying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you issue a report to Mr. Cermak telling him about the condition of the trout farm and what you found there?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did report to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's Exhibit D1033. I don't propose to go into it in any further detail as it's dealt with in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can just have a look at Exhibit D2D00547. 65 ter 2D00547.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see this document dated the 18th of September?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it's -- it's headed Split Military District Command, Knin forward command post, and it's a proposal for commendation of the president of Croatia concerning tasks carried out after Storm, and a list of names there of the individuals and yourself who had been identified as part of your team for a commendation from the president. Were you aware that you had been put forward, you and your team, for a commendation in relation to the work that you had done?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you receive a commendation for your work?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we can see on -- if we go to page 2, a statement of reasons filed signed by the Knin garrison commander, General Cermak, and a description of the nature of the work that was involved. Thank you, no need to ask you further questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no objection but just to -- to make sure there are no misunderstandings in the transcript, the letter stems from the Knin garrison and is addressed to the Knin forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, my mistake, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document Exhibit D1735. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1735 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's all I need ask. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Kay, I have one question for you. You have more or less reconstructed the mobilisation history of this witness. Now we start mid-August asking for retroactive effect. Then you've shown us the 6th of September decision on the matter, which was then repeated -- the request was then repeated. Now, the 6th of September document refers to something, a document on the 4th of September, and that's apparently -- and I'm referring you to D17 -- is it -- no. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] D1028, the 6th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the one that refers to -- that's the rejection of the request for mobilisation. That refers to a document on 4th of September which we have not seen. So that to extent there seems to be a gap in the reconstruction. Is it your intention to produce that, or is there any specific reason why if not dealt with the 4th of September request, and you just jumped from mid-August to the 6th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just make things clear. Nothing is being hidden away from Your Honour because I want to make it clear that we just find the materials 15 years later that we find. And if a document is missing in chain of correspondents, it's not for want of looking by my team and me through various databases to try and pull together all -- all the links. Sometimes you -- we are unable to find a missing document and much time and energy goes into trying to make the link. So I do remind the Court that, that when we do put together links of -- of these documents, we're not trying to hide anything from the Court, if something is missing, we have actually done our best out of very dispirit sources from the Prosecution 65 ter list where you might find one document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if you say we don't have the document, that's the reason why it's not there, that explains your situation. And then, of course -- but it was presented immediately following the 18th of -- or the 19th of August request -- was it the 19th? I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 19th, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for us to note that there is a missing element in the reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. The passage is it goes mobilisation, refusal; then to the minister of defence, refusal; and then eventually it gets a -- a permission that is granted. That's the -- the journey of this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi would, have you a copy of this document of the 9th -- of the 4th of September?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't have it, but I can try to -- to get it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A complete picture is always better than a half-complete picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We would be absolutely grateful for that, but we have not been able to find anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the other Defence teams. Any questions, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Mr. Waespi, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Teskeredzic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is counsel for the Prosecution. Just for my information, Mr. Kay said Mr. Teskeredzic. I said Mr. Teskeredzic. What's the right way of pronouncing your name? Because I'd like to do it appropriately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Teskeredzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Teskeredzic. Did you have an academic degree?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I graduated from the school of veterinary medicine. I am an -- I have an MA in oceanology. I also have a Ph.D. at the Faculty of Agriculture, and I am a scientific advisor, which means that I am a full time university teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Because I also have difficulties to pronounce your name, so I will call you doctor if that's fine.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: That's quite okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I would like to start by clarifying your functions within the Croatian Army as I can see them from your witness statement, which is D1732 in paragraph 2. Now, I understand that in July 1991 you joined the Croatian Defence, and then you became the commander of the special de-mining and waterborne operations. From when to when were you the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: So from that first day, the date that you quoted, until the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Colonel Jerko Domancic was your deputy?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And was he also your deputy when you went with your team to Knin in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. He's the best expert, the top expert for explosives and mine clearance. This is why I always had him at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I understand that the members of your team whom you took with you in 1995 were also, by and large, the members you had when you commanded that unit between 1991 and 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Teskeredzic. Now, another point I wanted to clarify with you is in paragraph 4 of your statement where you say that you learned about the appointment of Mr. Cermak as the commander of the Knin garrison on the radio. Do you remember when that was and what the message was on the radio?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: As I stated here, I was interested in knowing what was going on. I was on holiday. When I learned that Mr. Cermak was appointed commander of the Knin garrison, I phoned him, an offered my assistance together with my colleagues in normalising life in Knin. It was a news item on the radio that I heard about him being appointed to that duty. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On what day was that? On the 6th of August, or on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: It was on the 5th of August, because I believe that I was already in Knin on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember which radio station it was that you listened to and heard that message?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: The Zagreb Radio or the TV. I believe it was even a TV broadcast. But those are the media I followed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you referred to the radio in the statement. It's media in the statement. Nothing more, nothing less. And the word "radio" for the first time appears on page 25, line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, in paragraph 4, line 5, it says, "Later I heard about his appointment on the radio as well."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. You're right. I focussed on the second line, which was incomplete. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 5 of your witness statement, where you state that on your way to Knin you stopped in Zadar and reported to General Gotovina's headquarters. Now, what kind of headquarter was that, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: There was the army that was under his command there. Since I was heading for a war zone, I wanted to be well-informed so that I do not happen to come across enemy forces. I wanted to know what the situation was like in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You talked to the duty officer. Do you remember his -- according to your witness statement. Do you remember his rank or his name?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I really do not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then you go on to say that you wanted to have an employee from that headquarters, I guess, assigned to you as, you know, somebody to guide you through that war zone. Was an employee assigned to you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Somebody did come along, but I cannot really remember who it was. There was the general excitement of the times, and 15 years later, I can hardly remember the faces, let alone names. I do remember a person accompanying me, since it was not all that safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that you informed your colleagues, Colonel Domancic, Mr. Tomsic, Ivo Maljur, and Mr. Vuk. And I think they were in Zagreb and in Hvar at the time. How did you contact them?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: By telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I think that I phoned them back in Osor, where I was. Initially I phoned them to find out what the situation was like. So as soon as I found out about Mr. Cermak's appointment, I was in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Osor, that was where you were, I think you said, on vacation?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where is that approximately?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Osor is a place on the island of Cres. It is located on the verge between the island of Cres and Losinj, and we have a house there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And looking at Split, is that north of Split or south of Split on the Croatian coast?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: North of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the team you described, these various names with Colonel Domancic as the deputy, you were the leader of that team; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let's go to -- briefly to your mobilisation again. It's been dealt with by -- by Mr. Kay. You were mobilised into the Knin military -- the Knin garrison. Is that correct? That's the VP number, the unit you were mobilised into, assigned into. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that was done at the request of General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then we know from D1027 - we don't need to pull that up again - that you started to work immediately on the 6th of August without the paperwork, without any formal authorisation from the authorities above Mr. Cermak being ready at that time. You started to work immediately.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So Mr. Cermak was clearly able to get in touch with you, or you got in touch with him, and make you and your team available to work with him without having, at that time, the authorisation of his superiors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 of your witness statement, you state that you responded to every request for assistance. Now, from whom did you receive these requests, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Of course, I do. There were people arriving who were returning to their homes. There were representatives of the electricity supply company, representatives of -- or, rather, members of military units who asked us to accompany them when they had to check the railway line because there weren't that many of them, and we did in fact go out to check the railway lines. We were volunteers, and we were there to respond to anyone's call. Our duty at the time was to help prevent any serious incident happening resulting in injury or damage to anyone or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was Lieutenant Vuk also part of your team?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let's look at D763, and we have seen this document already this morning. So this document shows that members of your team were ordered by General Cermak to do certain things. Is that correct? If you look at paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Given the huge amount of explosives and ammunition present in the area, there was need for all of it to be taken out, removed, and, thus, to remove the danger that threatened everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And General Cermak made Lieutenant Andjelko Vuk responsible according to this document to clear the facility and terrain in the village of Plavno as urgently as possible. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also served on -- on a commission that was established by General Cermak, as we see in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 9 of your witness statement, you address the personnel, I believe, and I want to talk a little bit about gentleman Modrusan and Dr. Margus. It was General Cermak who made it possible that these two gentlemen were made available to you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to D1119.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Here you see an order by General Cermak --

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: By General Cermak that Mr. Zvonko Modrusan, an employee of, I believe, your institute, to come and be placed at the disposal of the Knin garrison commander. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So Mr. Cermak was capable of organising people so you could do your job; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: He tried to bring in people who could help us deal with certain matters. In this case, it involved a fish farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And Mr. Modrusan, he showed up and helped you to deal with these issues of the fish farm; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the same is true with Dr. Margus. It's the same story. Mr. Cermak, he --

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- ordered him to come, and Mr. -- Dr. Margus actually showed up as well.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Ordered. Asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where do you see the word "ask" in D1119?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, he couldn't order him. He couldn't order the institute. It may have been an error on his part. Also in my case, he wrote an order whereas he should have written a request, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you agree with me that Mr. Cermak used the word "order"?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it -- to me, it seems to be an error, because who is it -- is he sending this to, really?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you see the -- this document for the first time?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No, no. I've seen the document. But, you see, he is sending an order but to the attention of the Rudjer Boskovic Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you told the Defence team when you were shown the order or after you were shown the order that you thought this was a mistake?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In my view, the Rudjer Boskovic Institute and the national park, they all came there of their own accord. What was required was a formal document that would relieve these people of their regular duties so that they could come and deal with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in paragraph 2 of this document you also say -- it also states that this order shall take effect immediately?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Because they were already there on the spot. We were already engaged in our activities, and those of us who went there had to have some sort of a paper, a formality so that we could engage in mine clearance so as to save lives, and in dealing with the fish farm to save the fish stock there. So there needed to be a formal document indicating that the stated individuals were engaged in such and such activities of clearance and maintenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago, I asked you whether you told the Defence that you thought this was a mistake, and you said yes, on line 12 of page 31. Now, when did you tell the Defence that you thought this order was a mistake? Or was that "yes" just an acknowledgment of my -- of my question?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Okay. Let me repeat the question. Did you tell the Defence whether you thought that this order of General Cermak was a mistake or an error on his part? Did you tell that to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, I don't think we discussed the matter at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Teskeredzic. Maybe we could --

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Teskeredzic [In English] My name is very difficult for other --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, let me call you doctor then again. Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President - that's easier to say - it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which gives you some time for training your mouth musculature, Mr. Waespi. We will have a break. Could you give us any indication as to how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not that much. About half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour. Then that opens the perspective of finishing the -- concluding the testimony of this witness relatively early today. Mr. Kay, is the next witness already stand by.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the next witness is on his way. He was being brought this morning because the estimates were that this witness would be a day. So the decision was made to bring him this morning rather than have a potential stay overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which has what consequence, that you have not spoken to him yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The consequence is, Your Honour, that we would finish early today and start that witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Teskeredzic, let's go to D765. I think you have seen the document this morning. It's a request for temporary transfer of a few people, including Mr. Andjelko Vuk, although, in English, his rank is major. I think he was a lieutenant, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No, he was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. The names here, Vuk, Plemencic, Perkovic, your son, Mr. Halas. Who suggested these names to -- to Mr. Cermak that they would be suitable to -- to work for you?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Let's move to another issue, and this is 65 ter 2136. Now, here, we have a letter dated 27th August, and it's addressed to the chief of the -- and I quote, "State Administration for the Protection of Natural Resources and Cultural Heritage." Perhaps you want to read the document quickly for yourself.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, it mentions in paragraph 1, equipment specified which apparently is in the possession of the chief of this institution. And it's to be delivered to the Knin garrison command to you, Mr. Teskeredzic. Now, what kind of equipment was that, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the military post that I belonged to previously. They borrowed to the -- the equipment to the state administration, to Mr. Marijan Orlic. When I left the army, the equipment was not returned. We remembered at that point that it should not stay in the domain of the state administration; rather, that it should be returned to the army. And this is the equipment, divers' equipment that was needed to check whether at the Roski waterfall, out in the field, there were any mines to be cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you eventually receive the missing equipment?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember whether General Cermak filed a report against Mr. Madar [phoen] as he announced in his letter?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall become Exhibit P2651. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2651 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Teskeredzic, you filed a number of reports to Mr. Cermak. In a sense, that you reported about the work you did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And we have seen examples this morning so we don't need to go into that any further. And we also saw this morning in D1735 that General Cermak proposed you and other members of your team to become a presidential award. You told us that you did not get the award. Do you have any knowledge why you didn't get the award?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't really think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you said in your witness statement that you weren't subordinated to Mr. Cermak. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I cooperated with him, I assisted him as a volunteer in attending to the conditions prevailing there, in order to enable the return of civilians as soon as possible. I asked him to help me arrange other individuals to arrive there so that we could deal with the matters that were urgent at the time, like, for instance, clearing up someone's driveway to their home, and such-like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you have testified, and we have seen these documents, including your statement, you were mobilized at the request of General Cermak; you were mobilized into his unit, the garrison command; you reported to him about your work; he provided equipment and even personnel to you; team members received instructions by him or his deputy. All of this suggests that you were, indeed, part of the garrison command and subordinated to Mr. Cermak. How do you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, a subordinate. His task was to normalise life, and we helped in him one aspect of this work. Of course, I had to tell him what it was that I was doing. It would have been absurd for me to work there as a volunteer with others without him being aware of what it is that we were doing. He, with his team, helped me and my associates come together, and these were really people who were qualified for the job. Some of them came directly from the units where they were mobilized, others came back from retirement, others from their workplace in the institute or the national park. We came together, and it was not the sort of strict working drill or discipline or anything of the sort. It was cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 of your witness statement you say that you don't know what Mr. Cermak's duties were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Well, what the duties were. His task was to make the civilian infrastructure operational, to have the electricity and water supply running, to have the town cleared of mines, et cetera. I didn't have a feeling that he was there to do anything else. He did receive delegations that came to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you don't really know what his formal authorities were over other units or -- or other people. That's not something you could testify about.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't have any authorities over other units, as far as I was able to see from my stay there. It was more of a cooperation that he had with Pero Pasic, with the civilian population, he had contacted with UNPROFOR. That's something I was able to see as well. And that I believe that that was the direction in which his tasks tended to go. He did not have command over the police or the units that passed through there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to the fish farm, D1033. You have seen the document this morning, and I'm interested in a passage where you suggest, after visiting the farm, you suggest to General Cermak to engage military police for a 24-hour watch, to do, among other issues, to protect the fish.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. My view was that we had to take care of that, but in -- as far as I saw it, it was the military police and not Cermak who were suppose to guard and secure an area that still had a military presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The reference I'm interested in is on page 2 in both versions, English and B/C/S, just after the listing of these 15 pools. In paragraph 1, you see reference to the military police. Now, did the military police show up? Did they protect the fish, as you had suggested?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't the military police; it was Mr. Zdenko Roman who rotated with Margus and Zvonko Modrusan. They took turns and stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So Mr. Cermak, he denied your proposal to have military police organised for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Or he was unable to accommodate my request. I didn't think about it. Although there wasn't that much danger there while -- when we first came and cleared the area, what was left to us only was to maintain the condition which the fish farm was, and the people were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Teskeredzic. Let's go to a last issue; that's the damage done to -- to Knin. Now, you have a number of specialisations, professional ones. You're an expert of oceanology; you are a scientist who studies fish breeding; you are an ichthyologist - hopefully I pronounced that right. These are all sciences related to marine sciences, marine biology. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: It has to do with the technology and biology of fish breeding and the health of aquatic organisms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you are certainly not an expert in assessing damage done by artillery or mortar shells; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I'm not an expert, but I can see what the damage is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in page 6 of your witness statement, you say that six houses were hit by shells. At least that's what you observed.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I toured the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 6, yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: We don't have it yet. I can't see paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yeah, the exhibit is D1732. And I can quote it: "Knin was practically intact. According to my observation, six houses had been hit by shells."

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Can it be enlarged. I can't read it. There ought to be a second part as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, once you have digested the first three lines, we will move on to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, and what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You stand by that, that you only observed six houses damaged by -- or hit by shells when you toured Knin.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an approximation. There may have been another one. But I can still clearly describe where each of these houses was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, were you aware that a provisional UN assessment has listed 44 buildings as damaged by shelling? This is P64.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: That is possible. I wasn't aware of it. What I found and what is written here is the result of my observation of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you accept that others might come to different observations.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: They might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have a few questions for you, Mr. Teskeredzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You composed a team or a committee, in which Mr. Vuk was included. We've heard about Mr. Vuk. Mr. Gojevic -- when I say you, I meant to say that Mr. Cermak did so. You were a member of that team. Mr. Gojevic, do you know what his position was? It was Mr. Vuk who was supposed to report, apart from you, Mr. Gojevic and Mr. Vrkic were members. Do you remember that? We have seen this on the screen. I think it is -- is it D763 or is it D1020. Could the parties assist me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, it's D763.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we have D763 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe the witness gave, in paragraph 7, of his witness statement an answer to your question, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think he did yet, but ... Yes, you see this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Marin Frkic, do you remember to whom he was subordinated?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I believe -- well, I can't really remember. I know that Mr. Gojevic was a deputy to Mr. Cermak. And for the other one, for Mr. Frkic, I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But he was a colonel. But do you remember in what unit he was or ...

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. It's been a long time ago. I couldn't really even remember his name if it wasn't written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Gojevic, you remember that he was the deputy of Mr. Cermak. Do you have any recollection as to whether Mr. Frkic was also part of the garrison command, or was he an outsider?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Frkic? No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I help, Your Honour. D1023.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dated 9th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay, for that. You told us that you would receive requests for performing your tasks. We've also seen that in your report, that you give a brief survey of the performance of your task in de-mining, including military facilities. Do you remember from whom you got the requests to inspect those military facilities?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: We received such requests from different military personnel that would come there to take over the military depots so they would ask us to come if there were no de-miners at the Split command post, then they would ask us, or sometimes he would join them because they needed more persons for the particular tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can you remember whether you reported to those who made these requests to you, if not the garrison command?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No, we did not report to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you got a request from someone; for example, to inspect military apartments. Let me take you to this example. Do you remember from whom you got that request?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I really do not remember the details. People wanted to have their accommodation. They wanted to make sure that they will be safe. Different people would come and ask for our assistance, in order to make sure that there was nothing there that could inflict them any harm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you report on your work inspecting military apartments. Military apartments occupied by whom?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I really don't know who lived there. We went out when called, when this was arranged with the mine clearers from the Split area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said people wanted their houses to be inspected. Now, these military apartments, were they used by the troops or the military personnel that had left?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you're reporting on having inspected quite a number of military apartments. Is it your testimony that you did not know whether these apartments were used by the Croatian military or by the ARSK military?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Croatian military could not have used them, because they only arrived at that time. Previously they were used by the army of Republika Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So may I then take it that you did not receive a request to inspect them by those who had lived in those apartments?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: When people came, they came back. In the meantime, between 1991 and 1995, many military apartments who were previously used by officers of the JNA who were Croats, they left, and after this period of time, they came back. Now, obviously in the meantime, somebody else lived in that apartment, probably also members of the military, but they were not Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which does not yet answer my question. My question is: Whether you received these requests from those who lived in those apartments or not. And you're telling us that people returned, and someone else had lived in apartments that were owned by them or were occupied by them previously. Now, do you remember who asked you, requested you, instructed you - whatever word you would use - to inspect those apartments?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: We received the requests from people who wanted to move in, so people who came back at the time. You probably know that at the time many people were forced out of Banja Luka, for example. They came to Knin, and they wanted to move into these apartments that used to be military apartments. So even those people from Banja Luka asked us to do that, because they wanted to move in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any request or order to inspect such apartments that came not from individuals but from persons with a certain authority?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have D1048, I think it is, on the screen. Have you had an opportunity to read it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please take your time.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this is, apparently -- now, let me ask you, have you seen such orders for inspecting or pyrotechnically inspecting apartments which were owned by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you are reporting that you did pyrotechnical inspection of apartments. Could you explain to us what the -- if at all, whether there's any relation between the work you did and the work which, apparently, you see ordered by Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This task was issued to the 14th Engineering. They asked us to go to Vitorog. He came by; he said, Are there any people who are free at the moment? Yes, there are, so let us go there to inspect that [realtime transcript read in error "there"]. There were also people who cleared the apartments. There were quite a lot of problems there, because the electricity supply in Knin was cut off. There were chambers full of meat which went rotten, and there were quite a lot of problems in connection to that, cleaning of such cold chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I asked you what the relation was between your work and this work. And then you said; they asked us to go to Vitorog. He came by and said, Are there any people free at the moment. Yes, there are, so let us go there to inspect there. Now, who came by?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaricevic or another gentleman who was also there. There were a couple of them who would come by and say, We need some help and also people came by who wanted to move in such apartments. So the requests came from different sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But now, were you involved in the implementation of this order in any way?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, indirectly because they would come by and ask us to carry out certain inspections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when I earlier asked you whether apartments, by whom you were requested that, you said it was just individuals who asked you. But apparently here it is not just a request from individuals but you were involved in the performance of inspection tasks in apartments which were ordered by authorities.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Well, the authorities there were made of military units, and they sort of requested our assistance. We were not obliged to do that, but since there were people who were able to carry out such inspections, we did assist them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you ever receive a request from Mr. Cermak which you said, No, I'm not going to perform the task you're asking me to perform?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: No, I never received such a request. He knew what our compatibilities were, what it was that we were able to do. He did not issue written orders to us because there was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that was not what I asked. Did you ever, when Mr. Cermak requested something, I was not talking about orders, did you ever say, No, we can't do it, or we do not want to do it?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: I don't believe there were any such situations. He never requested anything that we were not able to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you finally met all the requests he addressed to you. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In your statement, in paragraph 6 you say something about the destruction in the town of Drnis and Oklaj village. And I read the relevant portion. After the part of the statement which deals with the six buildings that had been hit by shells in the town of Knin you said: "For the sake of comparison, I went to the neighbouring town of Drnis and Oklaj village where I established that between 1991 and 1995 all the houses had been destroyed by the Republic of Serbian Krajina." I would like to know exactly what you meant there. Did you mean to say that all the houses were destroyed; or all the houses you saw being destroyed were destroyed by the Republic of the Serbian Krajina? Could you elaborate on that sentence.

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Drnis and Oklaj are Croatian settlements and in 1991, when they were occupied by the enemy forces everything was destroyed and burned down. When I came I could see that this indeed happened back then in 1991 because over the three or four years, the vegetation started to grow out of these destroyed buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So no house was left intact in Drnis. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: Most of the houses. The impression was, as if everything was destroyed. Possibly here and there, there was a house that was intact, but most of the houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In paragraph 18 of your statement, you say something about a lady who had told you that: "... the leaving of the area and going to Serbia had been planned and organised." Did she give you any further details?

utterances.speaker: EMIN TESKEREDZIC
utterances.text: She did not only say this to me personally. I went there with a team from my institute, some four or five years ago. We did some research at the river Una near Donji Lapac, and personally I was interested in this. She came back. She was president of the fishing association there. And at the same time she worked at the Red Cross in Donji Lapac. So I asked her, I believe her name was Zorica, and I asked what happened at the time, and I described in detail what she told me. As I said she didn't address only me personally, but there were four or five of us from my team from the institute. So she said that a group of people came and shouted, the Ustashas are coming, they're going to slaughter everybody, so they moved towards Banja Luka.
